pages.title: Understand Archtree in 15 minutes
pages.description: A guided route from the system map to the code you will change.

sections.title: One backend, several experiences
body: Archtree manages the shared music and video catalog, account services, media delivery, and private listener features. Finitude is the listening experience built on those contracts.

This guide explains the implementation in this repository. Follow each source link to inspect the corresponding code. Business rules remain the authority for product behavior; this guide is a reading map.

items.text: React routes and one persistent player consume the listener APIs.

items.title: Identity
items.text: Sessions and viewer fences protect every private account operation.

items.title: Catalog + Content Manager
items.text: Administrators curate shared content; listeners receive ready public projections.

items.title: Media + storage
items.text: MongoDB records ownership and lifecycle; S3 holds the media bytes.

items.title: Library + Playlists
items.text: Private saves, history, and ordered collections belong to one account.

items.title: Social + rooms
items.text: Explicit participation, recoverable commands, and authorized realtime updates.

pages.title: Run Archtree locally
pages.description: Prepare the tools, configure a development environment, and recognize a healthy start.

sections.title: Start with the checked-in runtime
body: Use Node.js 24 and the patch recorded in .nvmrc. Install dependencies from the lockfile with npm ci. A different Node major is rejected by the test and build preflight.

The development checks require a trusted MongoDB daemon for disposable integration databases. Room audio analysis also requires FFmpeg with the documented decoding capabilities. The doctor command checks tools without reading application secrets or connecting to the application database.

sections.title: Configure a private development environment
body: Read .env.example for configuration names and the README for each setting. Create a local .env only when one does not already exist, or supply settings through the process environment. Keep values out of source control and diagnostic reports.

DB_CONN_STRING and DB_NAME select the intended development database. It must provide writable replica-set or mongos transactions. Authentication needs JWT_SECRET; storage, mail, and optional providers have their own settings. A passing doctor check does not supply these services.
Use a development database you are authorized to change. Application startup initializes required indexes and recovery state; the disposable test daemon does not become your development database.

steps.title: Start Express
steps.text: Run npm run dev from the repository root. With the default port, open http://localhost:8080. The landing page links to Finitude and available account actions.

steps.title: Start Finitude hot reload
steps.text: In another terminal, run npm run dev:web and open http://localhost:5173/finitude/. Vite proxies API requests to Express at 127.0.0.1:8080. If you change the server port, align the proxy configuration.

steps.title: Check the built experience
steps.text: Run npm run build, then use the Express /finitude route to inspect the generated listener bundle and deep links. A missing bundle and an empty catalog are different problems.

code.text:
npm run dev
# In a separate terminal:
npm run dev:web

sections.title: Know what success looks like
body: A successful server start reports server_listening. Check /health for the connected application database, required indexes, and topology. A running Vite server alone does not establish API readiness.

You should be able to open the listener without signing in. An empty development catalog can be a valid empty state. Content Manager at /content/manage requires an administrator account; public registration never creates one.

If startup fails, use the fixed stage, reason, and action fields in server_start_failed. Resolve the named configuration, topology, index, or port problem without pasting credential-bearing driver output.

callout.title: The first verification loop
callout.text: Run npm test and npm run build before handing off an implementation. Add the MongoDB integration and browser gates required by the behavior you changed.

pages.title: See the whole system
pages.description: Understand the running surfaces before choosing a folder or abstraction.

items.title: Public listener API
items.text: /api/listener/v1 returns bounded, allowlisted catalog and composition DTOs. Private endpoints apply account guards.

items.title: Finitude Web
items.text: /finitude serves the built React application; development uses Vite with same-origin API proxies.

items.title: Content Manager
items.text: /content/manage renders administrator workflows for metadata, relationships, uploads, and recovery.

items.title: Account + social APIs
items.text: /auth handles identity; /api/social/v1 provides explicitly enabled social and Audio room capabilities.

sections.title: The code has several established patterns
body: Routes compose transport guards and handlers. Controllers interpret HTTP input and response behavior. Services coordinate catalog reads, storage, identity, and lifecycle work. Models include persistence behavior rather than being plain type declarations.

Some newer workflows use application modules and focused repositories. Catalog publication uses these boundaries; social and rooms have application services and document types. Listener catalog reads currently query MongoDB directly from listenerContentService.
Trace the path you are changing before introducing a new layer. Do not assume that every endpoint follows Route → Controller → Service → Repository.

sections.title: Know which system owns the state

items.title: MongoDB
items.text: Owns catalog identity, accounts, references, lifecycle evidence, and durable command outcomes.

items.title: S3
items.text: Stores object bytes. Object existence alone never grants public catalog visibility.

items.title: HTTP
items.text: Handles reads and durable mutations, with ownership and retry rules at the relevant boundary.

items.title: WebSocket
items.text: Pushes authorized room updates; durable room state stays on the server.

items.title: Browser player
items.text: Owns the local media element and execution state while following server room authority when admitted.

items.title: Native clients
items.text: Consume shared contracts; device-local download and system playback rules are separately defined.

sections.title: Read contracts at the boundary
body: docs/business-rules.md defines agreed product behavior across clients. src/contracts contains versioned wire types; Web response schemas validate incoming JSON. Contract fixtures exercise old and current response shapes.

docs/architecture.md contains detailed implementation material and rollout context. Proposal files under docs/plans are sequencing or future work, not automatic evidence that a feature exists or is deployed.

pages.title: Catalog and Content Manager
pages.description: Shared content has public read projections and administrator-only mutation paths.

sections.title: Separate curation from listening
body: Artists, Organizations, Albums, MediaTracks, Credits, and configured page items describe the shared catalog. Content Manager provides server-rendered administration; Finitude reads listener-specific DTOs.

Only the exact persisted admin role grants shared-content mutation access. createdBy records provenance and does not grant ownership permissions. Ready public content is readable regardless of the viewer role.

sections.title: Find public content at its projection
body: listenerContentService resolves listener Home, search, Album, Artist, and track data. publicCatalogService serves legacy public catalog projections. Both must preserve ready visibility and avoid leaking persistence fields.

MediaTrack is the product identity. Existing audioTracks collections and audioTrack relationship values remain compatibility names and may also describe Video. Do not infer the media kind from those names.
Canonical Credits describe attribution. Compatibility artistIds and albumIds remain server-maintained projections during migration; they are not interchangeable with every credit role.

sections.title: Follow publication and references together
body: Catalog creation, artwork ownership, and relationship updates have recovery paths. Inspect publication and reference-fence services alongside the controller. A successful upload can precede a failed linking step and must remain recoverable.
Album membership order derives from embedded Track Numbers, with deterministic fallback ordering. The read layer preserves declared order; it does not invent a new order from query results.
Configured Home sections use persisted Carousel, Grid, and List definitions. A personalized section resolves against its authorized viewer and must not become a shared cached account response.

sections.title: Read the tests with the implementation
body: Use listenerContent.integration.ts for the ready-only public read contract and catalogCreatePublication tests for partial publication outcomes. Relationship, deletion, and lifecycle changes also require MongoDB integration verification.

pages.title: Identity and account boundaries
pages.description: A valid identity must stay valid through sessions, account transitions, and delayed responses.

sections.title: Authentication is more than a login screen
body: The auth routes cover password sign-in, email verification and recovery, configured federated providers, passkeys, sessions, and account actions. Capability endpoints determine which optional methods a client can advertise.

Short-lived access credentials are bound to revocable server sessions. Browser flows use HttpOnly cookies; native requests use their supported token contracts. Do not move browser credentials into ordinary client application state.

sections.title: Protect the account the user is viewing
body: Private browser requests carry a current account-viewer identity in addition to cookies. The server rejects a missing or stale viewer before reading or changing private data. Resource IDs alone never authorize access.

The browser coordinates shared-cookie transitions across tabs and removes the old account from the UI and caches immediately. Operation epochs prevent late responses from restoring the previous account after a switch.
Login and refresh install credentials under the shared session-transition lock. Review that coordination before changing retries or logout behavior.

sections.title: Account exit has dependent lifecycles
body: Account deletion includes sessions, private collections, and social relationships. Existing avatar and shared-catalog provenance blockers are product rules, not incidental database failures.

Changing a password, resetting it, revoking a session, and signing out everywhere have different retention rules. Test their effect on private data and active room controllers, not only the immediate HTTP response.

items.title: Login or refresh
items.text: Auth routes → authController → authSessionService; then browser session coordination.

items.title: Private data leak or stale account UI
items.text: Current-viewer guard → accountEpoch → the affected query cache and mutation.

items.title: Account removal
items.text: Account deletion service → dependent collection and asset lifecycles → integration tests.

pages.title: Media, storage, and recovery
pages.description: Publishing a playable file is a coordinated database and object-storage operation.

sections.title: A MediaTrack has one active media kind
body: Each MediaTrack has one ready media object and one active audio or video kind. Replacement preserves its catalog identity, saves, and Playlist memberships while changing the active object.
Public metadata and stream delivery require a database-confirmed ready object whose key is bound to the correct MediaTrack and kind. Finding bytes in S3 is not enough to serve them.

steps.title: Create
steps.text: Record recoverable ownership and pending lifecycle state before storing bytes. Publish only after storage and required content relationships are ready.

steps.title: Replace
steps.text: Validate and upload the replacement, atomically promote its identity, then clean up the old object. Failed cleanup retains exact evidence for later reconciliation.

steps.title: Delete
steps.text: Remove owned storage through the deletion lifecycle and clean references idempotently. Retain the final database evidence until storage cleanup is confirmed.

steps.title: Recover
steps.text: Distinguish a known failure from an uncertain outcome. Audit first and reuse the documented retry identity; an audit does not authorize deleting unknown objects.

sections.title: Delivery and room eligibility are separate
body: Media delivery includes bounded streaming, byte-range behavior, and concurrency admission. Replacing a file must preserve seek and retry correctness, not just return a new URL.

Ordinary playback does not imply room eligibility. Shared Audio needs source-specific duration and seekability evidence, including full compressed-input structure and decoding checks. Unsupported analysis must not break ordinary playback.

sections.title: Test the failure between two systems
body: Cover upload success followed by database failure, replacement promotion and cleanup failures, deletion retries, and concurrent reference changes. These are integration concerns even if the user-facing form change looks small.
Use the documented integration suite and relevant playback E2E gate. Successful fixture decoding does not establish deployed playback, background execution, or actual device audio output.

pages.title: Library, activity, and Playlists
pages.description: Three related features keep distinct ownership and mutation rules.

items.title: Saved content
items.text: Save and Unsave are collection preference state. Saving an Album does not save each MediaTrack; the saved collection is not limited to 20 items.

items.title: Recently Played
items.text: The latest 20 activity identities are independent of saves and Playlist membership. Explicit launch and automatic queue advancement have different reporting rules.

items.title: Playlists
items.text: An owner-only ordered set of MediaTracks. Playback copies ready members into the player queue; later edits do not rewrite that running queue.

sections.title: Read and mutate as the owner
body: Listener Library reads are guarded by authentication and the current viewer. The public catalog projection still filters content visibility inside private collections.

Playlist routes live under /content/me/playlists. Mutations use Idempotency-Key, and revision-dependent operations also require If-Match. An uncertain mutation must preserve its retry identity rather than become a second operation.
Unavailable Playlist members retain their stored positions but do not become playable queue items. Playlist artwork is a projection of usable member artwork, not a separate uploaded asset.

sections.title: The Web view has separate recovery states
body: Web Library offers My Playlists, Saved music, and Recently played. One failing section must not hide working sections or present itself as an empty collection.
Web is streaming-only. Native Library and downloads have additional device-local rules; a browser cache is not a Finitude download lifecycle.
Private query keys and mutations must remain tied to their account during logout or switching. Inspect account isolation alongside optimistic updates.

sections.title: Useful starting tests
body: Review Playlist integration tests for ownership, idempotency, and revision conflicts. Review lifecycle integration tests before changing content removal. Web page and mutation-isolation tests cover the corresponding presentation and account boundary.

pages.title: Social and shared Audio rooms
pages.description: Private social identity and durable room authority extend the existing listener.

sections.title: Feature presence is not rollout status
body: Social participation is explicit and separate from the private account profile. Friendships, direct music shares, and listening-status sharing have independent visibility and revocation rules.

Audio room support is implemented behind explicit capabilities in Finitude Web. Production rollout, native room screens, and shared Video remain separate delivery or verification stages. Check current capability responses before treating a screen as available.

sections.title: Commands and updates have different jobs
body: HTTP carries durable room commands and authorized snapshots. A command uses its original server-issued scope and command ID so retrying an uncertain result cannot duplicate the operation.
Room mutation processing records durable outcomes transactionally. Room persistence writes an outbox invalidation in the same transaction; the realtime gateway pushes current authorized state.
Reconnection must recover current authority before local playback can resume. Observer devices do not become controllers just because they receive the same room updates.

sections.title: Use the existing player
body: A room has its own server-owned queue and timeline, while each client executes audio through its existing single player. Local callbacks must not independently advance shared state.
The online room source is pinned to a media revision and requires verified eligibility. Readiness, local pause, permission changes, stale connections, and media replacement all constrain playback.
Room management, shared playback control, and personal volume or pause are separate permissions. Do not turn a snapshot or reconnect into a user gesture.

sections.title: Verify both durable state and client behavior
body: Room lifecycle and realtime integration tests cover authority, membership, and revocation. Web room tests cover recovery and the controls using that state. Browser playback gates and deployed checks remain necessary evidence for actual audio behavior.

pages.title: Finitude Web
pages.description: A routed React application with validated server data and one long-lived player.

sections.title: Start at the shell and route map
body: web/src/main.tsx installs localization, query state, browser session coordination, and the router. The application shell frames feature routes, while the player lives across navigation.

Feature folders organize Home, Search, Catalog, Library, Playlists, account flows, and social screens. API modules own request construction and response schemas. Follow the relevant route into its feature before changing shared shell state.

sections.title: Keep one player across routes and media kinds
body: The shared player owns queue, elapsed time, transport, media kind, Shuffle, and Repeat. Audio and Video use the same long-lived media element. Visual surfaces subscribe to that state rather than creating another player.
Launching playback and reporting Recently Played are explicit policies. Album Play, a selected track, and automatic advancement must not accidentally report the same activity.
Account transitions clear private caches but do not stop an already-playing public stream. Room transitions have additional authority and local-pause rules.

sources.label: Web behavior contract
sources.find: The Web listener renders administrator-configured Carousel, Grid, and List

sections.title: Edit canonical translation sources
body: Interface messages come from localization/catalog.json and localization/locales. Update canonical sources, validate them, regenerate outputs, then sync native resources when the shared contract changes. Do not hand-edit generated bundles.
Runtime bundles validate completely before activation. A failed remote language update preserves the readable current bundle; the packaged en-US bundle provides the final fallback.

code.text:
npm run localization:check
npm run localization:generate
npm run localization:sync-native

sections.title: Check behavior in the rendered application
body: Component tests exercise route and state behavior; Playwright covers navigation, playback, and accessibility in browsers. For UI changes, inspect loading, empty, failed, signed-out, keyboard, and narrow-screen states.
The Web build enforces initial JavaScript and static asset budgets. Keep new onboarding or administration surfaces from adding unnecessary code to the listener entry bundle.

sections.title: Ask the same questions at every boundary

steps.title: Who can make this request?
steps.text: Locate authentication, account scope, role guards, origin checks, and rate or size limits before the handler.

steps.title: Which state is authoritative?
steps.text: Find the canonical order, revision, lifecycle status, and ownership record. Distinguish a database record from its public DTO.

steps.title: What happens after a partial failure?
steps.text: Determine whether retry reads state, reuses an operation identity, or must reconcile an uncertain write.

steps.title: How does the client know it succeeded?
steps.text: Inspect the response parser, cache update, visible error state, and tests. A successful HTTP response is one boundary, not the whole user experience.

pages.title: Trace an Album from URL to screen
pages.description: GET /api/listener/v1/albums/:id is a small path that reveals several important boundaries.

sections.title: The path you will follow
body: AlbumPage → listenerAlbumQuery → apiRequest → listener route → album controller → listenerContentService → MongoDB → allowlisted DTO → response schema → AlbumPage.
This read is public. Opening the page does not save the Album, report playback activity, or fetch the media stream. Personal Save status and an explicit Play action use separate paths.

steps.title: 1. Mount the public route
steps.text: createApp mounts listenerRoutes at /api/listener/v1. The /albums/:id route applies publicReadRateLimit and asyncHandler. It does not require a login or account-viewer header.

steps.title: 2. Convert the HTTP request into a read
steps.text: The album controller trims the route ID and calls getListenerAlbum. An unavailable result becomes 404. A successful projection is returned as JSON with Cache-Control: public, max-age=60.

steps.title: 3. Validate identity and Album visibility
steps.text: getListenerAlbum accepts a 24-character hexadecimal ID and normalizes it. Its bounded MongoDB query requires a ready Album lifecycle, while explicitly supporting older records that have no lifecycleStatus. Missing and non-ready Albums return no projection.

steps.title: 4. Resolve only the canonical ready tracks
steps.text: When audioTrackIds is populated, the service normalizes and deduplicates its bounded ID list, fetches ready tracks, then restores declared order. It skips missing or non-ready entries and does not append reverse-linked tracks. Only a legacy Album without lifecycleStatus and with no declared IDs uses the albumId fallback, ordered by title and ID. A lifecycle-managed Album with an empty list stays empty.

steps.title: 5. Construct the listener DTO
steps.text: Catalog context resolves artwork and attribution. toAlbumSummary and toAudioTrackSummary explicitly construct { album, tracks } using listener fields. Storage keys, createdBy, lifecycle errors, and account data do not belong in that response. Each track has one mediaType and streamUrl.

steps.title: 6. Validate the response at runtime
steps.text: getListenerAlbum encodes the ID into a same-origin path and calls apiRequest with listenerAlbumSchema. The parser validates known fields and enum values while stripping unknown additive response fields. A malformed payload becomes an invalid-response error, not unchecked page state.

steps.title: 7. Render data, loading, or recovery
steps.text: AlbumPage uses the query result for metadata and the ready-track list. Failed reads expose a retry action. Save status is queried separately for the resolved account, and a Save-status failure does not convert public catalog data into a failed Album read.

steps.title: 8. Start playback only on a gesture
steps.text: The Album Play button passes the ready ordered tracks to launchAlbumPlayback. Reading the Album alone never starts audio. The launch policy records the Album activity identity; queue advancement follows its separate activity rules.

sections.title: Inspect evidence for the boundary you change
body: The listener integration suite requests the real Album endpoint without a session, asserts canonical ready-track order, and recursively checks for unsafe response fields. Its seeded content includes pending, unpublished, and missing references.

The Web compatibility tests parse legacy and current Album fixtures, strip future additive fields, and reject invalid known values. These tests complement the server DTO checks; they do not prove a deployed database contains the expected Album.

callout.title: A useful first exercise
callout.text: Choose one Album field and identify its stored input, public projection, response type, client schema, and visible use. Keep private persistence fields out of the DTO even if the client would ignore them.

pages.title: Make and verify a change
pages.description: Use the product contract, follow the actual implementation, and report the evidence you have.

steps.title: Read the behavior contract
steps.text: Read AGENTS.md and the relevant business-rules section before planning or editing behavior. An agreed rule change belongs in the canonical document with the implementation; identify conflicts before changing the contract.

steps.title: Trace the owned boundary
steps.text: Follow the route, authorization, application or service code, model, projection, and client parser that actually participate. Inspect the sibling clients when the shared behavior affects them; record any unavailable verification.

steps.title: Implement the behavior and its recovery
steps.text: Preserve unrelated work. Include tests for changed state transitions, ownership, retries, and cleanup. For storage or reference work, map create, replace, delete, partial failure, retry, and reconciliation before editing.

steps.title: Update the durable explanation
steps.text: Update README or the existing operational document when commands, settings, routes, authentication, media, or deployment change. Keep proposal status distinct from shipped behavior; avoid one-off verification reports.

steps.title: Verify and review the final diff
steps.text: Run the relevant gates, inspect dependency changes and the complete diff, and report skipped or unavailable checks explicitly. Temporary plan documents should be removed after completion.

sections.title: Choose checks by the affected behavior

items.title: Every completed implementation
items.text: npm test and npm run build; also run git diff --check and review the final diff.

items.title: Database, auth persistence, storage, or references
items.text: npm run test:integration uses a disposable MongoDB replica set and exercises durable failure paths.

items.title: Listener routes, UI, auth, playback, or accessibility
items.text: Run the relevant Listener E2E gate. npm run test:e2e:chromium is the faster browser gate; release-facing work uses the full matrix.

items.title: Release and deployment work
items.text: Follow the release matrix and Linux workflow for all browser engines, platform hooks, and artifact validation. Local macOS or Windows success does not replace Linux proof.

code.text:
npm test
npm run build
# When the changed behavior requires them:
npm run test:integration
npm run test:e2e:chromium
git diff --check

sections.title: Coordinate shared contracts
body: Use versioned response contracts and representative old/current fixtures when evolving the API. Additive response compatibility does not permit an invalid known enum or a changed meaning for an existing field.

Read the sibling Finitude iOS and Android implementations for a shared change. Native build, device execution, offline state, and background audio are different verification gates. This guide links repository-owned sources and does not claim native parity was verified by a Web test.
Translations are authored in the canonical catalog and locale files. Generate and sync derived artifacts using the checked-in commands, then verify the receiving clients.

sections.title: Make the result reviewable
body: Explain what changed, the user-visible result, the commands that ran, and their results. Separate local tests, CI, deployed checks, real-account behavior, and physical-device evidence.

A missing tool or unavailable environment is a skipped gate with a reason, never a pass. Keep secrets, personal configuration, generated reports, recordings, and dependency directories out of commits.
